translations.text: Often the solitary man waits for grace, the Measurer's mercy, though he, troubled in heart, has long had to stir the ice-cold sea with his hands across the waterways and travel the paths of exile. Fate is wholly fixed!
So spoke the earth-walker, mindful of hardships, of cruel slaughters, of the fall of dear kinsmen:
"Often I have had to lament my sorrow alone, every dawn. There is now no one living to whom I dare speak my mind plainly.
I know for a truth that it is a noble custom in a man that he bind fast his heart's enclosure, keep close his treasure-chamber [of thought], whatever he may think.
The weary mind cannot withstand fate, nor can the troubled spirit bring about help.

Therefore those eager for glory often bind a sorrowful mind fast in their breast-chamber. So I, often wretched, deprived of my homeland, far from my noble kinsmen, have had to fasten my mind with fetters,

since long ago I covered my gold-friend in the darkness of the earth, and I, wretched, went from there, winter-sorrowful, over the binding of the waves; dreary, I sought the hall of a giver of treasure,
[seeking] where, far or near, I might find one who in the mead-hall would know of my people, or would comfort me in my friendlessness and entice me with joys.
He who has experienced it knows how cruel a companion sorrow is to one who has few dear protectors.
The path of exile holds him, not twisted gold at all; a frozen spirit-enclosure, not at all the glory of the earth.
He remembers the hall-retainers and the receiving of treasure, how in his youth his gold-friend accustomed him to feasting. All joy has perished!
Therefore he knows, he who must long go without the counsels of his beloved lord and friend, when sorrow and sleep together often bind the wretched solitary man.
It seems to him in his mind that he embraces and kisses his lord, and lays his hands and head on his knee, as he at times did before, in days of old, when he enjoyed the gift-throne.
Then the friendless man wakes again and sees before him the dark waves, the sea-birds bathing and spreading their feathers, frost and snow falling, mingled with hail.

Then the wounds of the heart are all the heavier, sore with longing for the beloved one. Sorrow is renewed when the memory of kinsmen passes through his mind; he greets them with joyful words, eagerly gazes on the companions of men. They swim away again!
The spirit of those floating ones does not bring there many familiar utterances. Care is renewed for him who must very often send his weary heart over the binding of the waves.
Therefore I cannot think why in this world my mind should not grow dark when I consider all the life of men, how they suddenly gave up the hall-floor, the proud young thanes.
So this middle-earth, each and every day, declines and falls; therefore a man cannot become wise before he has had his share of winters in the kingdom of the world.

A wise man must be patient; he must not be too hot-hearted, nor too hasty of speech, nor too weak a warrior, nor too reckless, nor too fearful, nor too glad, nor too greedy for wealth, nor ever too eager for boasting, before he knows clearly.
A man must wait, when he makes a vow, until, bold in spirit, he knows clearly which way the thought of his heart will turn.

A wise man must perceive how ghostly it will be when all the wealth of this world stands waste, as now in various places throughout this middle-earth walls stand blown by the wind, covered with frost, the buildings storm-beaten.
The wine-halls crumble; the rulers lie deprived of joy; the whole troop has fallen, proud by the wall.
Some war took away, carried off on the road forth; one a bird carried off over the high sea; one the grey wolf gave over to death; one a sad-faced nobleman hid in an earth-pit.
So the Creator of men laid waste this dwelling-place, until, deprived of the noises of the townspeople, the old works of giants stood empty.
He then who has wisely considered this place of walls and deeply ponders this dark life, wise in spirit, often remembers from far back a multitude of slaughters, and speaks these words:
"Where has the horse gone? Where has the young warrior gone? Where has the giver of treasure gone?
Where have the seats of the feasts gone? Where are the joys of the hall?
Alas, bright cup! Alas, mail-clad warrior!
Alas, the glory of the prince! How that time has passed away, grown dark under the helmet of night, as if it had never been.
Now, in the track of the dear troop, there stands a wall, wondrously high, decorated with serpent shapes.
The noblemen were taken away by the might of ash-spears, weapons greedy for slaughter, fate the glorious; and storms beat against these stone cliffs, the falling snowstorm binds the earth,
the tumult of winter; then darkness comes, the night-shadow grows dark, sends from the north a fierce hailstorm in hostility to men.
All the kingdom of earth is full of hardship; the ordinance of fate changes the world under the heavens.
Here wealth is fleeting, here a friend is fleeting, here a man is fleeting, here a kinsman is fleeting; all this foundation of the earth will become empty!"
So spoke the man wise in mind; he sat apart by himself in private meditation.
Good is he who keeps his faith; a man must never make known the grief of his breast too quickly, unless he, a nobleman, knows beforehand how to bring about the remedy with courage.
It will be well for him who seeks mercy, comfort from the Father in heaven, where all our security stands.
